title: System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC
summary: The Microsoft Management Console is a signed Windows host process that loads administrative user-interface modules called snap-ins, described by console files with the .msc extension. Because the host is trusted and is normally seen performing administration, an adversary who can control its command line gains signed binary proxy execution without dropping a new executable. The straightforward abuse is argument-level: passing a built-in console such as the backup console with a silent or non-interactive argument performs a destructive administrative action, for example deleting the backup catalog so that recovery becomes impossible. A more layered abuse builds a console that references a Component Object Model class through the console's link handling, registers a matching class identifier under the registry, and then launches the console in embedded mode so the class is instantiated and its code runs inside the trusted host. Legitimate console use in an enterprise is highly predictable: consoles come from the Windows system directory or from a managed administrative share, run in an interactive session, and rarely spawn further processes. Detection therefore leans on command-line and parent-child process telemetry, on the rarity of the console file path or hash across the estate, and on registry class identifiers that appear alongside the console but have no installed software behind them.

beginner.definition: The Microsoft Management Console is the window Windows uses for many administrative tools. It reads small configuration files, called console files, that tell it which tools to show. Attackers can craft these files, or reuse the built-in ones, so the trusted console does their work for them.
beginner.whyItMatters: The console is a trusted Windows program, so blocking it is difficult without breaking administration. Attackers can use it to run damaging tasks quietly, such as removing the backup records that you would need to restore a server. It can also be made to load a harmful component that hides inside the trusted program. If you only watch for strange new files, this activity looks like normal administration.
howItWorks: The attacker obtains a way to run commands, then looks for a console file that performs a useful action.
The console is started with arguments that suppress questions, so a destructive task runs without a warning.
Another approach registers a class identifier in the registry that points to the attacker's component.
A console file is built that links to that class, for example through its web link setting.
The console is launched in embedded mode, which makes it create the attacker's component inside itself.
Telemetry shows a trusted console starting, running from an odd path, and spawning or loading extra code.
beginner.example: Think of a large office building where cleaners push a genuine branded trolley through every floor. Security waves them past because the trolley and the uniform are the real thing. One evening the trolley is loaded with tools that open the safe instead of cleaning supplies. The guards see the usual trolley at the usual time and log it as routine maintenance. Nothing about the trolley itself was fake, which is exactly why nobody questioned what it carried.
takeaways: Trusted administrative tools can perform destructive work through their own arguments.
A console file stored outside the usual Windows folders deserves a closer look.
Log the parent process of anything a console starts, because it rarely starts anything.

objectives: Explain how the management console host loads administrative modules from console files.
Identify command-line patterns that indicate a console file is being abused rather than used normally.
Describe how a registry class identifier can be used to make the console load attacker code.
Name the telemetry sources that record console execution and what it spawns.
Compare normal administrative console use with suspicious use from unusual paths.
